Option reference

Every option below can be given on the command line or set in the configuration file. Command-line values win where the two disagree.

Command-line options

--read-timeout

How long to wait for the first byte of a response, in seconds. The default is thirty. Setting it to zero waits forever, which is almost never what you want on a network you do not control.

--max-redirects

How many redirects to follow before giving up. The default is ten. A loop between two addresses is detected before the limit is reached and reported as a loop rather than as an exhausted budget.

--retry-backoff

The multiplier applied to the wait between retries. The default is two, meaning each retry waits twice as long as the one before it. Values below one are rejected because they would retry faster under load.

Environment variables

CACHE_DIR

Where to keep downloaded artifacts between runs. Defaults to a directory under the user's cache location. A relative path is resolved against the working directory at startup, not at use.

STRICT_MODE

When set to any non-empty value, a warning becomes an error and the process exits with status sixty-five. It is intended for continuous integration, where a warning nobody reads is the same as no warning at all.

Notes

Options are read once at startup. Changing the configuration file while the process is running has no effect until it is restarted.

An option given twice on the command line takes its last value, without a warning, because shell wrappers legitimately append arguments.

Unknown options are an error rather than a warning, in every mode. An option that is silently ignored is indistinguishable from one that did nothing.

The configuration file is parsed strictly: a trailing comma, an unquoted string containing a colon, or a duplicated key all stop startup with the line number reported.

Values are not expanded. A dollar sign in a configuration value is a dollar sign, and a tilde is a tilde, so a path meant to reach a home directory has to be written out in full.

Times are accepted in seconds only. There is no suffix syntax, deliberately, because the two common conventions disagree about whether m means minutes or milliseconds.
